lessons.title: Your values
lessons.summary: What matters to you in a smoke-free life?

slides.title: What does your compass show?
slides.text: Values are your compass for what matters in life: health, family, freedom, curiosity, hard work. Goals end one day; values always guide you.

slides.title: Why does it matter?
slides.text: When an urge comes, asking "Does this cigarette bring me closer to what I care about, or further away?" makes your decision easier.

slides.title: Make it concrete
slides.text: A concrete sentence like "To be able to run with my daughter" instead of "health" is a stronger reminder in a hard moment.

slides.title: You don't have to be perfect
slides.text: Living by your values isn't being flawless every day; it's turning back towards them each time.

practice.title: Practice
practice.text: Choose the two values that matter most to you and, for each, write something you want to do in a smoke-free life. You can add these sentences to your reasons.

quiz.q: How do values help when an urge comes?
options: They wipe out the urge completely
They make me ask whether the cigarette brings me closer to what I care about
They're just motivational words
quiz.explain: Values don't erase the urge, but by reminding you which way you want to go, they make choosing easier.

lessons.title: The urge is a wave
lessons.summary: The nature of an urge: it rises, peaks and fades.

slides.title: How does an urge behave?
slides.text: The urge to smoke is like a wave: it rises, reaches a peak and then falls. Most urges peak within a few minutes.

slides.title: Time is on your side
slides.text: When you don't respond to the urge right away, the wave fades by itself. Each time, your brain learns that the urge can pass.

slides.title: It gets rarer over time
slides.text: In the first days, urges are frequent and strong. As the weeks pass, both how often they come and how strong they are decrease.
slides.didYouKnow: Withdrawal symptoms are usually most intense in the first week and decrease markedly within the first month.

slides.title: Surf instead of fighting
slides.text: Fighting the urge can make it bigger. Noticing it and staying with it lets the wave pass.

practice.title: Practice
practice.text: Next time an urge comes, check the time and observe how long it lasts. You'll often find it's shorter than you thought.

quiz.q: How does the urge to smoke usually progress?
options: It keeps rising until you smoke
It rises, peaks and fades by itself
It never changes
quiz.explain: Urges are like waves; when you don't respond, they fade by themselves after the peak.

lessons.title: Urge surfing practice
lessons.summary: Learn to stay with the urge through guided practice.

slides.title: 1. Notice
slides.text: When an urge comes, tell yourself: "Right now I feel an urge to smoke." Naming it lets you see the urge without getting carried away by it.

slides.title: 2. Find it in your body
slides.text: Where in your body do you feel the urge? Chest, throat, hands, stomach? Explore the shape, temperature and intensity of the feeling with curiosity.

slides.title: 3. Accompany it with your breath
slides.text: Let your breath flow naturally. With each breath, make a little more room for the urge; don't try to push it away or chase it off.

slides.title: 4. Watch the wave
slides.text: The feeling may grow, change or fade. Just watch. When the peak has passed, you've ridden out a wave without smoking.

practice.title: Practice
practice.text: During an urge, watch it like a wave for 3 minutes: notice its rise, peak and fall. If you like, do it together with the breathing in the "I have a craving" tool. Even if there's no urge, practise once today.

quiz.q: What is the aim of urge surfing?
options: To get rid of the urge
To stay with the urge and let it pass
To force yourself to put off smoking
quiz.explain: The aim isn't to erase the urge but to stay with it; that's also the core skill in the iCanQuit study.

lessons.title: Thoughts are just thoughts
lessons.summary: Get some distance from the thought "Just one won't hurt".

slides.title: Your mind talks
slides.text: While you're quitting, the mind comes up with persuasive lines: "Just one won't hurt", "You deserve it today", "You can't quit with this stress".

slides.title: Thought ≠ fact
slides.text: A thought coming to mind doesn't mean it's true or that you have to follow it.

slides.title: Label it
slides.text: Say the thought like this: "I'm having the thought 'just one won't hurt'." This small sentence puts distance between you and the thought.

slides.title: The passenger in the back seat
slides.text: Think of your thoughts as passengers in the back seat of a car. They can talk, but you're at the wheel.
slides.didYouKnow: Starting again after "just one" is one of the experiences most often described by people who've tried to quit.

practice.title: Practice
practice.text: Today, when a thought about smoking comes, repeat it with "I'm having the thought that:" in front. Notice the difference you feel.

quiz.q: What helps when the thought "Just one won't hurt" comes?
options: Arguing with the thought and defeating it
Noticing it as a thought and letting it pass without following it
Smoking one until the thought passes
quiz.explain: Noticing and labelling the thought reminds you that you don't have to follow it.

lessons.title: Accepting physical sensations
lessons.summary: Being able to stay with tension, restlessness and a feeling of emptiness.

slides.title: Your body talks
slides.text: When you quit, you may feel tension, restlessness, empty hands or a knot in your stomach. These are normal parts of withdrawal.

slides.title: Resistance makes it bigger
slides.text: Trying to get rid of an uncomfortable feeling right away often makes it more noticeable.

slides.title: Make room
slides.text: Instead of fixing the feeling, try making room for it: "This feeling can be here, and I can carry on with my day alongside it."

slides.title: It's temporary
slides.text: Physical withdrawal sensations usually decrease within a few weeks. Every day your body gets more used to a nicotine-free balance.

practice.title: Practice
practice.text: Today, when you feel discomfort, just observe it for 60 seconds: where, what is it like, how strong? Then see what has changed.

quiz.q: What is the ACT way of dealing with an uncomfortable physical sensation?
options: Trying to get rid of it right away
Making room for it and carrying on with it
Ignoring it and suppressing it
quiz.explain: Acceptance isn't liking the feeling; it's making room for it and continuing to do what matters to you.

slides.title: Smoking was a tool for emotions
slides.text: Many people use cigarettes to cope with stress, anger or boredom. When you quit, these feelings become more visible.

slides.title: Smoking doesn't solve stress
slides.text: The relaxing feeling of a cigarette comes largely from relieving nicotine withdrawal. A while after quitting, many people feel calmer.

slides.title: Name the feeling
slides.text: Saying "I'm angry right now" or "I'm bored" puts a little distance between you and the feeling and makes choosing easier.

slides.title: New tools
slides.text: A short walk, a breathing exercise, talking to someone or writing the feeling down are ways that can take the place of smoking.

practice.title: Practice
practice.text: Today, when you have a strong feeling, name it and try a tool instead of a cigarette: breathing, a walk or writing to someone.

quiz.q: What is the main reason smoking seems to reduce stress?
options: Cigarettes are a calming drug
Nicotine withdrawal is temporarily relieved
The smoke relaxes the lungs
quiz.explain: A smoker goes through mild withdrawal between cigarettes; a cigarette relieves it, so it feels relaxing.

lessons.title: Willingness
lessons.summary: Making room for discomfort for the sake of what matters to you.

slides.title: What is willingness?
slides.text: Willingness is being prepared to make room for uncomfortable feelings and thoughts for the sake of something that matters to you.

slides.title: Like climbing a mountain
slides.text: Someone who wants to reach the summit doesn't like being tired, but accepts it. A smoke-free life also means accepting some hard moments.

slides.title: All or nothing
slides.text: Willingness is like a switch: on or off. Instead of trying to reduce the urge, you can choose to open the door to it.

slides.title: Connect it to your values
slides.text: The answer to "Why am I willing to accept this difficulty?" lies in your values.

practice.title: Practice
practice.text: Today, during an urge, ask yourself: "Am I willing to make room for this discomfort for what matters to me?" Note your answer.

options: Liking the urge
Being prepared to make room for discomfort for what matters to you
Giving in to the urge
quiz.explain: Willingness isn't liking the discomfort; it's choosing to make room for it for the sake of your values.

lessons.title: What to expect from withdrawal
lessons.summary: Symptoms, how long they last and ways to cope.

slides.title: The first days
slides.text: Symptoms usually peak in the first few days after quitting. The first week is the hardest period.

slides.title: Common symptoms
slides.text: The urge to smoke, irritability, restlessness, trouble concentrating, sleep problems and increased appetite are the most common.

slides.title: How long does it last?
slides.text: Most symptoms decrease markedly within the first month. Irritability is most intense in the first week and can last 2–4 weeks.
slides.didYouKnow: Withdrawal symptoms are a sign that your body is getting used to living without nicotine; they're temporary.

slides.title: Coping
slides.text: The symptom tips in the daily check give short suggestions for each symptom. Getting support also makes withdrawal easier.

practice.title: Practice
practice.text: In today's check, mark the symptoms you feel and try one of the suggestions.

quiz.q: When are withdrawal symptoms usually most intense?
options: A year after quitting
In the first days after quitting
They never decrease
quiz.explain: Symptoms usually peak in the first days and decrease markedly within the first month.

slides.title: A worry, a fact
slides.text: Some people may gain a little weight after quitting. The reasons include increased appetite and small changes in metabolism.

slides.title: The gain is bigger
slides.text: The health benefits of quitting smoking are far greater than the possible effects of a few kilos.

slides.title: Small strategies
slides.text: Not skipping meals, keeping fruit and vegetables handy, drinking water and moving a little every day help.

slides.title: Stay smoke-free first
slides.text: In the first weeks, your priority is staying smoke-free. You can make bigger changes to your diet when you feel stronger.

practice.title: Practice
practice.text: Choose and prepare two healthy snacks to have handy tomorrow.

quiz.q: What's the best approach to weight worries in the first weeks?
options: Starting a strict diet
Making staying smoke-free the priority and taking small, sustainable steps
Going back to smoking so as not to gain weight
quiz.explain: Small steps are enough; the real gain is staying smoke-free.

slides.title: Settings trigger
slides.text: Social settings where people smoke, weddings, cafés and gatherings with alcohol are strong triggers.

slides.title: Short and clear
slides.text: "Thanks, I've quit" is enough. You don't have to explain.

slides.title: Plan ahead
slides.text: Before you go, think about what you'll drink, where you'll stand and what you'll say if someone offers you a cigarette.

slides.title: Careful with alcohol
slides.text: Alcohol can weaken your resolve. In the first weeks, avoiding settings with alcohol or keeping them limited makes things easier.

practice.title: Practice
practice.text: Write an If–Then plan for a social situation you might face this week and say your "no" sentence out loud once.

quiz.q: What might be the most useful answer when someone offers you a cigarette?
options: Giving a long explanation
A short, clear sentence like "Thanks, I've quit"
Taking one but not smoking it
quiz.explain: A short, clear answer leaves no room for debate and strengthens your decision.

lessons.title: A slip isn't a collapse
lessons.summary: Self-compassion and getting back on track.

slides.title: Slips can happen
slides.text: Smoking one or a few cigarettes is common while quitting. It doesn't mean the journey is over.

slides.title: The "I've already blown it" trap
slides.text: The biggest risk is giving up on quitting altogether after one cigarette, thinking "I've already blown it".

slides.title: Self-compassion
slides.text: Treat yourself as you would a friend. Instead of blaming yourself, try to understand what happened.

slides.title: Learn and carry on
slides.text: Find the trigger for the slip, make a new plan for it and carry on with the programme. Your total smoke-free days are kept.

practice.title: Practice
practice.text: Write the answer to "What will I do if I slip?" now: log it, look at why, make a new plan, carry on.

quiz.q: What is the most useful step after a slip?
options: Blaming yourself and leaving the programme
Understanding what happened, making a new plan and carrying on
Acting as if nothing happened
quiz.explain: Learning from a slip and carrying on is an important part of the quitting journey.

slides.title: Identity changes
slides.text: There's a small but powerful difference between "someone trying to quit smoking" and "a non-smoker".

slides.title: Change your language
slides.text: Saying "I don't smoke" instead of "I can't smoke" reminds you that the choice is yours.

slides.title: Every choice is a vote
slides.text: Every smoke-free day is like a vote for the person you want to be. As the votes add up, your new identity grows stronger.

slides.title: The long term
slides.text: Over time, smoking stops being part of your life. Even after this camp ends, it's important to keep up your new habits.

practice.title: Practice
practice.text: At least once today, introduce yourself or think of yourself as "a non-smoker".

quiz.q: Which sentence supports your new identity more?
options: "I can't smoke"
"I don't smoke"
"I'm not smoking for now, but..."
quiz.explain: Saying "I don't smoke" emphasises that the choice is yours and strengthens your new identity.

lessons.title: Smoking, blood vessels and sexual health
lessons.summary: Bonus lesson: how quitting affects your blood vessels and sexual health.

slides.title: Smoking affects blood vessels
slides.text: Substances in cigarette smoke damage the inner lining of blood vessels and can narrow them. This reduces blood flow.

slides.title: The link with sexual health
slides.text: An erection depends on enough blood flow to the penis. That's why smoking is one of the known risk factors for erection problems.

slides.title: When you quit
slides.text: Quitting smoking improves circulation. Over time some people also see improvements in sexual health; however, this varies from person to person.

slides.title: When to see a doctor?
slides.text: Ongoing erection problems may be related to heart and blood vessel health. In that case it's important to see a doctor.

practice.title: Practice
practice.text: Today, go for a 10-minute brisk walk. Movement supports circulation too.

quiz.q: How can smoking affect sexual health?
options: By narrowing blood vessels and reducing blood flow
It doesn't affect it at all
Only through the smell
quiz.explain: An erection depends on enough blood flow; smoking can make this harder by affecting the blood vessels.
